lesson.grammar_point: countable and uncountable nouns with how much, how many, a lot of, a few and a little

listenings.text: Good morning. I'm Tom, and I'm the data analyst on your account. Let's look at September. First, traffic. How much traffic did the website get? A lot: about eighty thousand visits. Most of it came from Google, and a little from Instagram. Now, leads. How many leads did the campaigns bring? Only four hundred, and that is not many for eighty thousand visits. So the conversion rate is low, half a percent. Here is the insight: the form on the website has twelve questions. That is too many. People start the form and then they leave. My advice is simple: make the form shorter, with only a few questions.

Hi, it's Priya again. I work for an online store that sells kitchen products. Last month we had a lot of visitors: about fifty thousand. Many of them looked at the products, and around five thousand put something in the cart. But only a few hundred people bought. So where is the problem? We looked at the funnel step by step, and we found it: a lot of people leave on the payment page. The page asks for too much information, and it is very slow on the phone. That was our insight. We don't need more traffic. We need a better payment page.

the people who see your posts when you do not pay
the percentage of people who do what you want, like buy
any moment when a customer meets the brand

reading.rtitle: Why Companies Have Data but No Insights
paras: Today almost every company has a lot of data. There is data from the website, from the CRM, from paid media and from social networks. Many companies also have a beautiful dashboard with twenty numbers on it. So why do so many managers still say: I don’t know what to do next?

The problem is simple. Data is not an insight. A dataset tells you what happened: how many people visited the website, how much money you spent, how many leads you got. An insight tells you why it happened and what to do. For example, a store sees that the conversion rate is very low. When the team looks at the funnel, they see that a lot of people leave on the payment page. That is an insight: the payment page is the problem, not the ads.

Good analysts look at the whole customer journey, not only at one touchpoint. They ask a few good questions before they open the numbers. And they choose only a few numbers for the dashboard: the ones that help the team decide. The result is less data on the screen, but a lot more action.
